A1.notes.Q3: As an advisor, I need data to help early, but Absalon tracking feels like surveillance without clear gains. Sensitive data is risky; use only if it fixes bias or aids specific vulnerable groups.
A1.notes.Q4: I cannot build trust or offer tailored advice if I don't understand why a student was flagged. High explainability is non-negotiable; black-box models are unacceptable regardless of accuracy.
A1.notes.Q5: Missing students in marginalized groups perpetuates inequality. I am willing to sacrifice some overall efficiency (up to ~5%) if it ensures we don't systematically overlook specific student demographics.
A1.notes.Q6: A combination of a warm generic nudge and an invitation is best. Continuous contact causes fatigue; twice per term balances urgency with respecting student autonomy.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic emails, casting a wider net helps awareness. For personalized advisor time, we must be precise to avoid stigmatizing students who are fine but flagged.
A1.Q8.1: We need to ensure the 'support' offered is actually available and not just an alert system that increases workload without resources for follow-up care.

A2.notes.Q3: Course performance is standard; Absalon data needs proof of value to justify privacy intrusion. Sensitive data only for fairness or critical support needs.
A2.notes.Q4: As an advisor, I need to explain 'why' to the student clearly. Without a clear reason, trust is lost and intervention fails.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount; we cannot miss marginalized students even if it slightly reduces total reach. We must balance recall and false positives equally.
A2.notes.Q6: Generic emails are easily ignored. A personalized approach with a low-threshold meeting invite is most effective for early support.
A2.notes.Q7: For generic info, cast a wide net. For personalized contact from me as an advisor, precision matters more to maintain credibility and avoid fatigue.
A2.Q8.1: The model must be reviewed regularly for bias drift. Also, students should have the right to see what data is used against them opt-in/out options where possible.

A3.notes.Q3: As an advisor, course performance is vital data. However, tracking digital behavior (Absalon) feels invasive and risks creating a surveillance culture that damages the trust I need to build with students.
A3.notes.Q4: I must be able to explain the 'why' to a student during our meeting. Without clear reasons, I cannot validate their experience or offer tailored advice effectively.
A3.notes.Q5: We must prioritize reaching vulnerable students across all groups. If a group is systematically missed, the system fails its ethical duty to support everyone equally.
A3.notes.Q6: Generic emails often get ignored. A personalized message followed by a voluntary invitation to talk is the most respectful and effective way to start support.
A3.notes.Q7: For generic info, casting a wider net is okay. But for personalized advice, I want high certainty to avoid overwhelming students who are actually doing well with unnecessary intervention.
A3.Q8.1: I am concerned about the stigma attached to being 'flagged'. If not handled carefully by advisors, the contact itself might feel punitive rather than supportive.

S1.notes.Q3: Having dropped out before, I know credit counts aren't enough. Grades matter less than engagement (Absalon), but tracking login data feels invasive unless it saves many students.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm flagged. A 'black box' would make me feel judged without a way to respond or understand the issue.
S1.notes.Q5: Missing vulnerable students is worse than contacting some who don't need help. Fairness means catching everyone, even if overall numbers drop slightly.
S1.notes.Q6: Generic emails are easy to ignore. A personalized note or a low-pressure meeting invite feels more human and less like spam.
S1.notes.Q7: With generic info, balance is key. But for personalized advice from an advisor, being slightly over-inclusive ensures no one in crisis slips through the cracks.
S1.Q8.1: The model shouldn't punish my past dropout or part-time work hours; it needs context to distinguish 'struggling' from 'juggling life'.

S2.notes.Q3: As an international student working part-time, financial data feels too invasive. Nationality helps tailor support for visa/cultural issues without harm.
S2.notes.Q4: Trust is vital for me. If I'm contacted, I need to know why clearly (High). Black-box models feel like surveillance.
S2.notes.Q5: International students often face unique barriers. We must prioritize reaching everyone equally over total numbers, even if it costs efficiency.
S2.notes.Q6: A generic email is low pressure; an invitation offers real help without forcing a conversation I might not be ready for.
S2.notes.Q7: Generic emails are less intrusive, so casting a wider net is okay. Personalized contact must be precise to avoid stigma or annoyance.
S2.Q8.1: The model should account for the cultural context of international students and not mistake adaptation struggles with lack of ability.

S3.notes.Q3: Using course performance is okay with gains, but tracking Absalon clicks feels like surveillance of my health condition. Sensitive data needs huge benefit or fairness justification.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged, especially with a health condition. 'Black box' models feel unfair and prevent me from addressing the root cause.
S3.notes.Q5: As someone in a marginalized group regarding ability, missing students is worse than false positives. We must ensure equal help reaches everyone who needs it.
S3.notes.Q6: Health crises happen suddenly; waiting for annual checks is dangerous. I prefer a gentle email or an optional meeting, not invasive calls.
S3.notes.Q7: A generic info spam is less harmful than missing someone in crisis. But personalized emails carry more stigma; they must be highly accurate to avoid distress.
S3.Q8.1: The definition of 'difficulty' matters: does it capture health-related needs or only academic performance? Also, who owns the prediction data?

S4.notes.Q3: Given my ADHD and past dropout, granular data helps catch struggles early. However, sensitive disability or demographic data feels invasive unless it directly improves fairness for marginalized groups.
S4.notes.Q4: With ADHD, I need to know exactly why I'm flagged (e.g., missed deadlines) to trust the system and take action. Black-box models feel like surveillance without a path to support.
S4.notes.Q5: Prioritizing recall is crucial for students with hidden disabilities or past dropouts; missing them once more could mean dropping out again permanently over fairness metrics.
S4.notes.Q6: I need low-friction, voluntary support immediately when struggles arise. Continuous monitoring with a choice to meet is better than waiting for annual check-ins.
S4.notes.Q7: Generic info has low cost of false positives. Personalized contact from an advisor needs higher precision so students don't feel wrongly judged or overwhelmed by unnecessary outreach.
S4.Q8.1: The system must ensure that being flagged does not create a 'digital file' affecting future applications or grading, especially for neurodivergent students.

S5.notes.Q3: As an international student, I worry about data on nationality or race being misused to stereotype us. Academic performance data is fine for support, but sensitive identity data feels intrusive unless it directly improves fairness.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to know why I am flagged, especially since Danish academic culture is different from my home country. Without a clear reason ('High' explainability), the contact feels like surveillance and damages trust.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness matters deeply for international students who might struggle differently due to language or cultural barriers. I would accept missing some total cases if it ensures the system doesn't systematically overlook our group.
S5.notes.Q6: I prefer a low-pressure generic email first, with an option for a meeting if needed. Continuous monitoring feels too invasive; checking twice a year balances support with my privacy.
S5.notes.Q7: A generic email to many is okay, but personalized messages from advisors should be reserved for clear cases. False positives in personal outreach can feel intrusive and stigmatizing.
S5.Q8.1: The model must account for cultural differences in study habits that might look like 'difficulties' but are actually normal adjustments for international students.

S6.notes.Q3: Having dropped out once, I value early help but fear surveillance. Course data is fine; 'Absalon' tracking feels invasive like spying on my struggle as an international student.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know *why* I am flagged, especially with a language barrier and prior dropout history. Black-box models would feel discriminatory and prevent me from trusting the support offered.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is critical for international students like myself who might be under-detected due to language or background differences. Missing us (false negatives) is worse than a false alarm.
S6.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and scary given my history. A personalized message or a voluntary invite to talk is better. Continuous checking helps because struggles can appear suddenly.
S6.notes.Q7: For generic info, I don't want spam if not struggling. For personalized advice from an advisor, a balance is needed; better to reach out than miss someone who needs help.
S6.Q8.1: The model must account for the transition shock of moving countries and language barriers. A prior dropout in another country shouldn't automatically flag me as 'at risk' without context.

S7.notes.Q3: As a dyslexic student, I fear Absalon tracking monitors my struggle strategies unnecessarily. Disability data is crucial for tailored support but must be protected; general demographic flags seem invasive unless proving fairness.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged to trust the process, especially with a disability. Black-box models feel like surveillance without transparency; high explainability is essential for my psychological safety.
S7.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help (like me) is worse than contacting some unnecessarily. I accept losing a few total identifications to ensure marginalized groups, including those with learning differences, are found equally.
S7.notes.Q6: A generic email is a low-pressure start, but a voluntary meeting offer feels supportive. Early intervention is key; waiting months for someone with learning difficulties to fail exams before helping is too late.
S7.notes.Q7: For generic emails, fewer false positives prevent spam fatigue. For personalized advice from advisors, a balanced approach ensures no one slips through the cracks without overwhelming resources.
S7.Q8.1: Students with disabilities often have atypical study patterns (e.g., slower reading speed) that might look like 'risk' data to an algorithm but are just accommodations in action. The model must distinguish between struggle and disability-specific strategies.

S8.notes.Q3: As a Faroese student who once dropped out, I fear surveillance (Absalon data) but need support for first-gen or financial struggles. Disability/First-Gen data must be used to help equity.
S8.notes.Q4: Trust is fragile after my dropout experience. I need to know exactly why I am flagged ('clear reasons') to accept help without feeling stigmatized by an opaque algorithm.
S8.notes.Q5: If a system misses minority students like me, it fails its purpose. I would rather have fewer total catches than ensure marginalized groups are disproportionately overlooked by the model.
S8.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel like spam and might trigger my dropout anxiety again. I need a human connection or specific, tailored advice to re-engage with the university support.
S8.notes.Q7: A generic email shouldn't disturb too many people (spam risk). A personalized message is valuable enough that balancing reach and precision is acceptable to avoid missing anyone in need.
S8.Q8.1: Ensure advisors are trained not to stigmatize students flagged by algorithms; the 'why' matters as much as the detection. Also, allow opt-out for those who prefer self-directed help.

S9.notes.Q3: I worry about surveillance (Absalon). Disability data feels too risky; I fear stigma if the system misinterprets my health condition.
S9.notes.Q4: As a student with mental health struggles, I need to understand why I'm flagged. Trust is essential for me to accept help.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness matters: marginalized students (like international ones) must not be missed more often. Prioritize finding everyone who needs help equally.
S9.notes.Q6: I prefer low-pressure options like an email or voluntary meeting. I don't want unsolicited calls, but early contact is crucial for my situation.
S9.notes.Q7: For generic emails, avoid spamming everyone. For personalized advice from an advisor, aim for balance; I value their time but need timely support.
S9.Q8.1: Crucial to ensure the 'support' offered is actually accessible and non-stigmatizing. My condition requires flexibility that standard deadlines don't allow.
